title: Population-scale immune multiome atlas reveals regulatory disease mechanisms.
data_url: gs://finngen-public-data-multiome (https://storage.googleapis.com/finngen-public-data-multiome/README.md); browser https://cascade.finngen.fi/; access form https://www.finngen.fi/en/access_results

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Listed the public Google Cloud bucket finngen-public-data-multiome anonymously (no login): 6,433 objects, 682 GB total (eQTL 340 GB, caQTL 248 GB, accessibility tracks 90 GB, peak-gene links 3.8 GB, CASCADE 45 MB, coloc 293 MB). Read the 17.9 KB README, which documents every column. Downloaded and parsed (pandas, first try): manifest (6,431 rows with sizes and MD5); CASCADE variant table, 119,094 rows, 0 duplicate variants, 89.5% single-base changes, 46,475 inside a peak; CASCADE peak table 297,024 rows; CASCADE gene table 27,294 rows; PBMC (all-cell pseudobulk) caQTL peak table 297,024 rows, 185,928 at q<0.05; PBMC eQTL gene table 27,236 rows, 18,050 at q<0.05; PBMC chr1 caQTL credible-set file 27,202 sets, 18,995 pass purity, 3,328 single-variant; consensus peaks BED 298,224 rows; R12 eQTL colocalisation 82,931 rows. Ranged-read the first 400 KB of the PBMC chr22 caQTL fine-mapping file: 66 columns including beta, se and posterior inclusion probability per variant-peak pair.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: From the abstract and search snippets only: 10 million nuclei, 1,108 donors, 51,083 eQTLs, 338,100 caQTLs, 593,765 peak-gene links, and the MPRA (massively parallel reporter assay) validation of 10,428 QTLs. I found no MPRA data in the bucket and no accession for it (paper is paywalled, no PMC copy). I did not stream any multi-GB fine-mapping or nominal file, so the count of fine-mapped variants with effect sizes per cell type is not verified.

a1_downloadable.note: Verified: the bucket lists and downloads anonymously. The README says FinnGen 'asks' users to fill a free form at finngen.fi/en/access_results; it is a courtesy request, not a gate. Single-cell count matrices are controlled access through the FinnGen Sandbox (GDPR) and are not used here.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Verified in a file header: caQTL effect size (beta, se) and fine-mapping probability are columns of the SUSIE.snp files, per variant-peak pair per cell type. But these files are 32 GB for the PBMC set alone, so getting a label table means a streaming filter, not a download.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs are GRCh38 coordinates plus reference and alternate alleles (e.g. chr22_16522789_A_G), so DNA sequence comes from one local reference-genome file; no per-row lookups.

a4_units_stated.note: README states caQTL slope is in standard-deviation units of inverse-rank-normalised log2-CP10K accessibility, and warns eQTL betas (Poisson model) are not comparable.

a5_enough_rows.note: Counted: 119,094 variants with fine-mapping probability >0.5 in the CASCADE table; 46,475 sit inside a peak. Per-cell-type counts with effect sizes not yet counted.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~1 GB after filtering (hg38 reference ~0.9 GB plus a <100 MB variant table); raw source to stream once is 32 GB (PBMC) to 180 GB (all cell types)
a6_fits_laptop.note: Estimated. Fits if you stream-filter the tabix-indexed fine-mapping files once and keep only high-probability rows; storing them is not feasible on the laptop's 50 MB-per-file policy.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Verified matches: 119,094 putative causal variants (abstract) equals CASCADE variant rows; 297,024 tested peaks equals README and peak table. Abstract's 210,584 caPeaks across cell types not recomputed.

a8_label_provenance.note: caQTL beta is a regression of measured accessibility on genotype across 1,108 donors, not another model's prediction. Caveats: which variants count as causal comes from SuSiE statistical fine-mapping, and the CASCADE mechanism category is derived from the QTL calls themselves, so using it as a label would be partly circular.

B1.why: Verified: labels split over 23 chromosome files per cell type; joins on variant_id and peak_id are documented.

B2.why: Verified: all nine downloaded tsv.gz/bed.gz files parsed in pandas on first try, no missing core fields.

B3.why: README: caQTL slopes all from one tensorQTL pipeline, same normalisation, SD units, across cell types.

B4.why: No censored values; effect sizes and P values are continuous numbers (seen in file header).

B5.why: No duplicate variants in CASCADE table (verified), but one variant maps to many peaks and cell types.

B6.why: Verified: README documents every column of every file type, including ID formats and coordinate conventions.

C1.why: Cell-type transfer question is informative either way; beating AlphaGenome on effect size is not.

C2.why: AlphaGenome and ChromBPNet are open and benchmarked on caQTLs, but not on this Finnish 24-cell-type set.

C3.why: Diversity: largest single-nucleus caQTL set, Finnish, 24 immune subtypes, released Aug 2026; likely unmodelled.

C4.why: Labels required multiome profiling of 1,108 donors; each new caQTL needs population-scale assays.

C5.why: AlphaGenome zero-shot scores give a ready baseline; sign-majority and per-cell-type mean dummies are obvious.

D1.why: AlphaGenome (weights released 2026) and Nucleotide Transformer are open-weight DNA models.

D2.why: Nucleotide Transformer embeddings cache on CPU; AlphaGenome 1 Mb context is slow on CPU.

D3.why: AlphaGenome non-commercial; Nucleotide Transformer CC BY-NC-SA; data has no stated licence.

E1.why: Hold out whole chromosomes, or hold out cell types, to stop linked-variant leakage.

E2.why: 23 chromosomes and 24 level-2 cell types available as groups (file listing verified).

E3.why: Majority effect sign, per-cell-type mean slope, and distance-to-peak-centre baselines are trivial.

E4.why: Standard error column per variant gives the noise floor; shared peaks across cell types act as replicates.

E5.why: Variants breaking known lineage motifs (SPI1/PU.1 in monocytes, CTCF) must show expected sign.

E6.why: Label shuffling within chromosome and allele-swap sign flip are straightforward.

E7.why: Other public caQTL sets (e.g. the Cell Genomics immune caQTL study) and the paper's MPRA, if located.

E8.why: No published model number on this exact set; paper's MPRA data not found in the bucket.

G1.why: Verified: GRCh38 coordinates with alleles, Ensembl gene IDs, consensus peak coordinates.

G2.why: gnomAD constraint by Ensembl gene, GTEx eQTLs and Open Targets by variant coordinates.

G3.why: Variant-to-peak-to-gene is one-to-many; needs a collapse rule (lead peak, best cell type).

G4.why: Constraint-versus-transmission question is the paper's own finding, so joining adds less new.

H1.why: Verified: all 297,024 tested peaks reported, incl. 111,096 non-significant in PBMC; low-probability variants kept.

H2.why: One population (Finnish), one tissue (blood), one sequencing centre; 24 cell types.

H3.why: Claim is precise: sequence predicts caQTL sign in Finnish blood cell types for well-powered variants.

H4.why: README states power filters, empty cell types, and eQTL/caQTL non-comparability explicitly.

I1.why: Kanai, Daly, Xavier groups (FinnGen) and Open Targets, which is ingesting this release (gentropy pull request).

I2.why: Would tell variant-interpretation pipelines which cell types sequence models fail in; marginal decision change.

I3.why: Sign accuracy and correlation roughly match how variant prioritisation uses these scores.

I4.why: Sequence-to-allelic-effect mapping is genuinely complex; no lookup reproduces it.

J1.why: Real modelling: frozen DNA embeddings, grouped splits, cross-cell-type transfer.

J2.why: Motif controls help sanity-check; immune regulatory genetics intuition needed for edge cases.

J3.why: Zero-shot benchmark table by cell type is shareable before any head is trained.

J4.why: No stated budget; roughly two to three weeks is plausible.

J5.why: No kill date written in NOTES.md.

existing_models.name: AlphaGenome, Google DeepMind's DNA sequence model predicting many genomic tracks from 1 Mb of sequence
existing_models.score_and_split: Search snippet of its paper: caQTL predicted-versus-observed effect size Pearson r 0.74 on fine-mapped caQTLs from other ancestries; not re-read or reproduced.

existing_models.name: ChromBPNet, a base-resolution convolutional model of chromatin accessibility
existing_models.score_and_split: Search snippet: variant scores correlated r=0.68 with allelic imbalance in African caQTL studies; used in a CD4+ T cell multi-QTL study (medRxiv 2026).

backbone.name: Nucleotide Transformer (DNA language model) embeddings of reference and alternate 1 kb windows; AlphaGenome zero-shot scores as comparator
backbone.hardware: CPU laptop for Nucleotide Transformer embeddings; AlphaGenome on CPU is slow, subset to a few thousand variants
backbone.licence: Nucleotide Transformer CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; AlphaGenome non-commercial

integration.partner_dataset: gnomAD gene constraint (LOEUF) and GTEx eQTL catalogue
integration.join_key: Ensembl gene ID; GRCh38 variant coordinates with alleles
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do sequence models predict accessibility effects equally well at constrained and unconstrained genes, or does their accuracy track the buffering the paper reports?

controls.positive_control: Variants that break SPI1/PU.1 motifs should close chromatin in monocytes; CTCF-motif variants should show consistent sign across cell types.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle labels within chromosome; flip ref/alt to confirm the predicted sign flips.
controls.external_validation: Another public immune caQTL set (Cell Genomics 2025 immune caQTL study) or the paper's MPRA results if their location is found.

honest_claim_h3: Among variants fine-mapped with high probability in blood from 1,108 Finnish donors, a frozen DNA-model head predicts the direction of their effect on chromatin accessibility in each of up to 24 immune cell types, and we measure how that accuracy transfers between cell types.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use the DNA sequence around a common genetic variant to predict whether it opens or closes chromatin in each blood immune cell type.
plain_idea.train_on: Reference and alternate DNA windows around each fine-mapped variant; 119,094 candidate variants verified, per-cell-type count with effect sizes unknown.
plain_idea.predict: The sign and size of the variant's effect on chromatin openness, measured by regressing accessibility on genotype across 1,108 donors' single-nucleus ATAC-seq (open-chromatin sequencing).
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Variant-interpretation groups (Open Targets, FinnGen) learn which immune cell types sequence models handle badly; a failure map is useful in its own right.

pitch.headline: Public, no-login caQTL effect sizes for 24 immune cell types from 1,108 donors, with 119,094 fine-mapped variants already tabulated.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: One pipeline, one normalisation, 297,024 peaks tested in every cell type with negatives kept; README documents every column. Finnish founder population adds enriched variants absent elsewhere.
pitch.the_win: A per-cell-type table showing where AlphaGenome's zero-shot sign accuracy drops, and whether a head trained on T-cell caQTLs transfers to monocytes.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: A cell-type-resolved benchmark of zero-shot sequence models on a fresh, unseen caQTL set, which nobody has published for this release.
pitch.who_wants_it: Kanai/Daly/Xavier FinnGen multiome team and Open Targets Genetics (ingesting this data) deciding how much to trust sequence-model scores per cell type.

ml_idea: Stream-filter the tabix-indexed SuSiE fine-mapping files to variants with posterior probability >0.9 inside a peak, take their caQTL beta per cell type, embed ref/alt 1 kb windows with a frozen DNA model, fit a per-cell-type head with chromosome holdout, and compare to AlphaGenome zero-shot and to cross-cell-type transfer.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, nothing timed: streaming 32 GB of PBMC fine-mapping files at ~10 MB/s is ~1 hour per cell-type set; about 50,000 variants x 2 alleles x ~0.2 s per window for Nucleotide Transformer on CPU gives ~6 hours.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Stream one chromosome's fine-mapping file for two cell types (e.g. CD14_Mono, CD4_Naive) and count single-base variants with probability >0.9 inside a peak; under ~1,500 genome-wide per cell type kills the per-cell-type design.

verdict_reason: Public, well-documented summary statistics pass Part A, but labels sit in 32-180 GB of tabix files needing a streaming filter, the per-cell-type count of usable fine-mapped variants is unverified, and caQTL effect prediction is already benchmarked by open models (AlphaGenome, ChromBPNet), so the value is a new cell-type-resolved benchmark rather than a new task.
